summary.text: Repeated-squaring computations show that the residue of 28341 has exact order 28341 modulo 283411 (excluding the quotients by the prime divisors 3, 47, and 67) and that its 28341st power is still 1 modulo \(283411^2\). Evaluating \(x^{28341}-1=\prod_{d\mid28341}\Phi_d(x)\) modulo \(283411^2\), exactness of the order makes every proper-divisor factor a unit, so the remaining cyclotomic factor must vanish modulo the square.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
n=28341,\qquad p=283411,\qquad M=p^2=80321794921,
\]
and let \(\Phi_m(X)\) denote the \(m\)-th cyclotomic polynomial. We prove that
\[
M\mid \Phi_n(n).
\]
This immediately gives the stated assertion for the sequence, since \(a(n)=|\Phi_n(n)|\).

We will use the standard cyclotomic factorization
\[
X^m-1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(X)                         \tag{1}
\]
for every positive integer \(m\). All the congruence computations below are ordinary repeated-squaring computations.

First, we record that \(p=283411\) is prime. For completeness, this can be established by the following primality certificate. We have
\[
p-1=283410=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5\cdot 47\cdot 67,
\]
and \(2,3,5,47,67\) are prime. Repeated squaring modulo \(p\), with base \(2\), gives
\[
2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and, for the distinct prime divisors \(q\) of \(p-1\), gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(p-1)/q&2^{(p-1)/q}\pmod p\\ \hline
2&141705&283410\\
3&94470&153836\\
5&56682&174613\\
47&6030&147198\\
67&4230&236184
\end{array}                                                    \tag{2}
\]
Each entry in the last column, after subtracting \(1\), is relatively prime to \(p\). Explicit Bézout certificates are
\[
\begin{aligned}
141705(283410-1)-141704(283411)&=1,\\
43191(153836-1)-23444(283411)&=1,\\
80838(174613-1)-49805(283411)&=1,\\
79994(147198-1)-41547(283411)&=1,\\
19773(236184-1)-16478(283411)&=1.
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{3}
\]
These data prove primality by the following elementary form of the Pocklington argument. If a prime \(r\) divided \(p\), then (2) and (3), reduced modulo \(r\), would show that the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(r\) divides \(p-1\), but does not divide \((p-1)/q\) for any prime \(q\mid p-1\). Hence that order contains the full power of every prime occurring in \(p-1\), so it equals \(p-1\). Since an element of \((\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z)^\times\) has order dividing \(r-1\), this gives \(p-1\mid r-1\), and therefore \(r\ge p\). A prime divisor of \(p\) cannot exceed \(p\), so \(r=p\). Thus \(p\) has no proper prime divisor and is prime.

We next determine the order of \(n=28341\) modulo \(p\). Notice that
\[
n=28341=3^2\cdot47\cdot67.                              \tag{4}
\]
The repeated squares of \(n\) modulo \(p\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\qquad}c|r}
e&n^e\pmod p&e&n^e\pmod p\\ \hline
1&28341&2&25507\\
4&178804&8&125739\\
16&213486&32&99053\\
64&91400&128&137364\\
256&214349&512&36125\\
1024&191381&2048&66576\\
4096&99147&8192&17074\\
16384&174968&&
\end{array}                                                     \tag{5}
\]
Every row follows from the preceding relevant entry by squaring and reducing modulo \(283411\). Multiplying the entries selected by the binary expansions of the exponents gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
\text{exponent}&\text{binary sum used}&n^{\text{exponent}}\pmod p\\ \hline
28341&16384+8192+2048+1024+512+128+32+16+4+1&1\\
9447&8192+1024+128+64+32+4+2+1&153836\\
603&512+64+16+8+2+1&168687\\
423&256+128+32+4+2+1&196258.
\end{array}                                                     \tag{6}
\]
For example, the first line can be checked by successively adding the selected exponents in the order
\[
1,5,21,53,181,693,1717,3765,11957,28341;
\]
the corresponding residues are
\[
28341,95484,161049,31640,89275,125606,247688,90664,6254,1.
\]
Thus the first line of (6) indeed gives
\[
n^n\equiv1\pmod p.                                       \tag{7}
\]
The other three residues in (6) are all different from \(1\). Since
\[
\frac n3=9447,\qquad \frac n{47}=603,\qquad \frac n{67}=423,
\]
we have
\[
n^{n/3}\not\equiv1,
\qquad n^{n/47}\not\equiv1,
\qquad n^{n/67}\not\equiv1\pmod p.                       \tag{8}
\]

It follows that the multiplicative order of \(n\) modulo \(p\) is exactly \(n\). Indeed, (7) says that the order divides \(n\). If it were a proper divisor of \(n\), then the quotient of \(n\) by the order would have a prime divisor \(q\). By (4), that prime would be one of \(3,47,67\), and the order would divide \(n/q\). This would imply \(n^{n/q}\equiv1\pmod p\), contradicting (8). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(n)=n.                                  \tag{9}
\]

We now use (9) to control all the cyclotomic factors indexed by proper divisors of \(n\). We claim that for every positive proper divisor \(d<n\) of \(n\),
\[
\Phi_d(n)\not\equiv0\pmod p.                               \tag{10}
\]
Suppose instead that \(\Phi_d(n)\equiv0\pmod p\). Applying (1) with \(m=d\), and evaluating at \(X=n\) modulo \(p\), gives
\[
n^d-1=\prod_{e\mid d}\Phi_e(n)\equiv0\pmod p,
\]
because the product contains the zero factor \(\Phi_d(n)\). Hence \(n^d\equiv1\pmod p\). By (9), the order \(n\) must then divide \(d\). But \(0<d<n\), which is impossible. This proves (10).

Since \(p\) is prime, (10) says that every integer \(\Phi_d(n)\), for a proper divisor \(d\) of \(n\), is relatively prime to \(p\), and consequently also relatively prime to \(p^2=M\). Therefore its residue modulo \(M\) is a unit. It follows that the product
\[
U:=\prod_{\substack{d\mid n\\d<n}}\Phi_d(n)                 \tag{11}
\]
is a unit in \(\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z\).

It remains to show that \(n^n\equiv1\pmod M\), not merely modulo \(p\). This is another repeated-squaring computation. The repeated squares modulo
\(M=80321794921\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
e&n^e\pmod M\\ \hline
1&28341\\
2&803212281\\
4&10305286175\\
8&56856623504\\
16&11119560660\\
32&34823658856\\
64&7305860158\\
128&72720565854\\
256&77339958728\\
512&48530202121\\
1024&18484540212\\
2048&77970117019\\
4096&39630026099\\
8192&23437256541\\
16384&8780247748.
\end{array}                                                     \tag{12}
\]
Using the same binary decomposition
\[
28341=1+4+16+32+128+512+1024+2048+8192+16384,
\]
and multiplying the selected residues in (12), reducing after each multiplication, gives the following cumulative check:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
\text{cumulative exponent}&n^{\text{cumulative exponent}}\pmod M\\ \hline
1&28341\\
5&12069152919\\
21&58902886234\\
53&3524814247\\
181&59346352675\\
693&71235197045\\
1717&8309007975\\
3765&79405617822\\
11957&20736622302\\
28341&1.
\end{array}                                                     \tag{13}
\]
Thus
\[
n^n\equiv1\pmod {p^2}.                                    \tag{14}
\]

Finally apply the cyclotomic factorization (1) with \(m=n\), evaluate at \(X=n\), and separate the divisor \(n\) itself from the proper divisors. We obtain the exact integer identity
\[
n^n-1
 =\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(n)
 =\Phi_n(n)\prod_{\substack{d\mid n\\d<n}}\Phi_d(n)
 =\Phi_n(n)U.                                                  \tag{15}
\]
Reduce (15) modulo \(M\). By (14), its left side is zero. Hence
\[
\Phi_n(n)U\equiv0\pmod M.
\]
But \(U\) is a unit modulo \(M\) by (10) and (11), so it can be cancelled. Therefore
\[
\Phi_n(n)\equiv0\pmod M.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
283411^2\mid \Phi_{28341}(28341).
\]
Divisibility of an integer by a positive integer is unchanged on taking absolute value, and the sequence term is
\(a(28341)=|\Phi_{28341}(28341)|\). Consequently
\[
\boxed{283411^2\mid a(28341)}.
\]
